On photograph number 2, you as the cameraman are standing to the right of the vehicle so that -- shall we say that piece of wood or whatever it is that is attached to the right part of the frame is facing inwards, is it, and cannot be seen? Do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number -- which number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, let me just see if you've got the same one on the screen that I've got. Yes. Now, you're standing to the right and you're facing towards the left and so the flap visible in number 3 would be away from the camera; is that correct? Do you see the one I'm talking about that is immediately adjacent to the right-hand edge of the box? That would be bent inwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 2 depicts the refrigerator lorry in the form in which it was removed from the Danube. No work had yet been done on the rear of the lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an original photograph of the original state of the lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On photograph number 3, you're standing at a different angle. You're standing to the left of the back of the truck and you are photographing into the side of the -- from the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So we're looking at it from two different angles.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I wonder in fact whether it would be more convenient to have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will give you more time. There's one matter which I've got to deal with before the break and that concerns the preparations for the programme tomorrow. We have a Pre-Trial Conference for Bosnia and Croatia. We also have to have a closed session hearing. What we propose is this: That we will have the Pre-Trial Conference at 9.00 tomorrow morning. It will be followed by the hearing in closed session, and then we'll continue with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I've been giving thought to what order of witnesses is most appropriate, given the two crime-base witnesses and K34 who are here to give evidence this week. Jemini, one of the two crime-base witnesses may in due course, I don't know, be the subject of a ruling that in part or whole can be given under 92 bis. And in any event, because he comes to deal with a particular matter raised in relation to an earlier witness's evidence, will be fairly short. It's really three passages of conversation that he has to give, and my strong temptation is to take him next in the hope that he will be finished effectively in one session, and then to turn to K34. My estimation is that K34's evidence will probably take, in chief, between one and two sessions. That will then stretch into tomorrow, leaving some of tomorrow and Friday for cross-examination, hopefully being in a position then to take the one outstanding crime-base witness at the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll look at Isuf Jemini. We've just been given the document in relation to him. We'll give a ruling about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. According to my list, no Jemini should follow now, but Musa Krasniqi. And I was told yesterday that K34 would be next followed by Musa Krasniqi, not Jemini or Jemini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a narrow point in the case of Mr. Jemini. We have to get K34 in. We'll look at it. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. Would you be back, please, Mr. Radojkovic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, before you sit down, could you please put this photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, during the break I found the original photograph rather than the copies that we've been dealing with. Would you look at that original photograph, number 3, as it were, in this series, and is that a clearer photograph? It doesn't seem to make much difference on the ELMO, I'm afraid. Is that the original photograph, sir, of this --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is an original photograph, and visibility is much better. You can clearly see the foot, the arm. The arm is less visible because -- but I see it because I saw it with my own eyes. Perhaps it's more difficult for you. Here is the arm, here is the foot and the other foot. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've shown this original photograph to the amici and also had an opportunity, through the court clerk, to show it to Mr. Milosevic. I wonder whether the usher could show it to Your Honours while I ask a couple of questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, just so that I'm clear about what you were saying, this photograph was taken once the truck had been pulled out of the river further than the previous photographs, photographs 1 and 2; is that correct? It's closer in on the bank?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken when the rear wheels or the rear part of the truck was already pulled out to the gravel bank of the river, and it is after this photograph that the patching was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm just going to ask some specific questions. When the truck was submerged in the water, did the box itself with the bodies, did it fill with water? Was there water inside as well as bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As you pulled the truck out of the water, did the water come out of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was precisely the difficulty in the course of extracting the lorry. The difficulty was that the trailer box was full of water, increasing the weight of the lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And in the process of the water escaping the box through the hole in the back, is that -- do you have any explanation as to how it is that the bodies are now shown and the flap is now -- seems to have been closed? Is that as a result of the force of the water coming out of the back of the box during the process of extraction?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The flap, the damage to the door had to occur earlier. The water could flow into the trailer box through other channels as well as through that opening. But in the process of extraction, the water flows out, and when the lorry is pulled out to a certain extent, the cable is dragging the truck and then the water resistance pushes back the door to its original position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And does that --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pushes back the flap.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And does that explain, to some degree, the reason why the flaps or the damage to the door looks different from photograph 2 to photograph 3?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you were extensively cross-examined with respect to the official notes of the working group for the MUP. Now, you did not prepare that document, did you? You're not the one who authored it.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You provided the information that is contained in that working note; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I gave that information verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You have recently had an opportunity to read the working notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw them in the hands of the OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you read those in the Cyrillic script --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tab 8, Your Honours, of the Exhibit 274.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- did you agree that what you told the working group was contained in that report? In other words, was the information they recorded accurate?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the OTP investigator, I said that I had read the Official Note, and I said it was accurate. I only had reservations about the second part of that statement. I said it was intended more for my colleagues, not the Tribunal. It was intended for my colleagues to follow up on the work that had already been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. It's not that the information was inaccurate; you didn't expect to see it in the report in our hands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information was provided to the working group to enable their continued operative work, that is, the checks they were running. I didn't expect to see it in a report before this Tribunal because they deal with hearsay and with rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the evidence in chief that you were asked to give in this courtroom by the Prosecution was restricted to that information about which you had personal knowledge, not hearsay or rumour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I testified about what I have done myself and what I have seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. There is some suggestion about the statement that you made. Sir, is what happened in the taking of your statement that you were -- that the original document that was produced was in English. There was a conversation in Serbian with the investigator, it was translated into English and then retranslated into Serbian. Is that what you understood happened, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First -- the first time I saw the Official Note it was in the Serbian language, and I was then shown an English translation of that Official Note, but I don't understand English and I cannot say whether it was a good translation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not talking now about the Official Note. I'm talking about a witness statement that you gave to investigator John Zdrilic on the 1st of June, 2002 and Monday the 3rd of June, 2002 in the presence of an interpreter whose name also appears. That's what I'm talking about. The original statement there was taken in English; is that correct? You're nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Final question: It was suggested to you by the accused that among these 86 bodies, and I'm talking now about the 17-to-20-year-old man, that there were no gunshot wounds. Can you explain to the Court what you mean by an entry/exit wound? When you talk about an entry/exit wound, do you mean a gunshot entry/exit wound, or some metal object entry -- tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the body of that young man, on the chest there was an entry/exit wound inflicted by a projectile. When you say an entry/exit wound, it means that a projectile or a bullet enters and exits the body on the other side. So you have an entry wound and an exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you able to determine from your experience whether or not that projectile was like a bullet or like a stake or some object? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that it was inflicted by a projectile, because I have seen many such injuries. A projectile is a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is the same young man who had, I believe you gave evidence earlier, that his hands were tied behind his back with wire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are all my questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the -- Mr. Nice, the future progress. We've considered the position. What we have in mind is we really ought to get on with K34 as soon as possible. I've discovered a document which suggests that counsel has been granted to him. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Counsel has been with him on all substantive proofing sessions. He wasn't there this morning when matters have just been gone over again. Yes, he has been available to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's limited to that. I mean, it's not proposed that counsel comes into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Then the next matter is this: That Mr. Jemini is here but being taken out of order. I gather it will take a little time to get K34 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to be sensible, for that to be put in hand, K34 to be got. But it may be that we can use the time for Mr. Jemini to start with, but it may be also that the accused isn't ready to cross-examine and we would find that understandable because, of course, the order has been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind to admit it, the statement, under Rule 92 bis. Of course, we will have to hear the accused on that and we will do so now, but what may happen is that we will have Mr. Jemini in chief and put the cross-examination off until tomorrow or a suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Entirely as Your Honour pleases. Although admitted under 92 bis, I will have to deal, of course, with the three particular conversations that he overheard, conversations he can speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, two matters. First of all, it's proposed that Mr. Isuf Jemini should give evidence or, rather, his statement should be admitted under the usual Rule, and we will hear you on that. The second matter is this: You may not be ready for cross-examination, in which case we would be prepared to put cross-examination in his case off until tomorrow or Friday so you would have time to prepare. So two questions for you to answer: Do you oppose the admission under Rule 92 bis, apart from your usual objection; and secondly, are you prepared to cross-examine now, or would you wish to cross-examine at a later date?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can cross-examine him today without delay, but I believe it makes sense for you to bear in mind although I did get his statement in due time, if what you are constantly curtailing you call time allowed, but I understand that you want me to cross-examine him under 92 bis, and I object to that because that radically, drastically shortens my cross-examination time. I understood that he would not be under 92 bis. I have prepared a large number of questions, prepared for a witness whom I expected to testify in the normal way, and then I see that he is introduced under 92 bis and my time is considerably shortened. So I agree to him being introduced under 92 bis, providing that you allow me enough time to cross-examine himself properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is Mr. Jemini, not Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have Krasniqi's statement, of course. I just protest against this practice of the OTP, who constantly keep changing the sequence of witnesses. But they cannot take me by surprise and find me unprepared to cross-examine witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have that in mind, that if there is an alteration, it may impact on your ability to prepare for cross-examination, and if you find a difficulty about it, then you must apply to us and we will consider whether to grant you time. But if you're ready to deal with Mr. Jemini, we will admit his statement under Rule 92 bis. I would anticipate the usual rules will apply about length, but in view of what you've said, we will consider the position during your cross-examination. Yes. Well, we'll hear Mr. Jemini then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he be brought into Court. And while that's being done, the Chamber may wish to refresh its memory in relation to the earlier relevant evidence. The map at page 10 and Exhibit 216 relate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the Court already has copies of the 92 -- Rule 92 bis package. May these be distributed to others who require them and may the witness please have a copy of the statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your full name Isuf Jemini?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, did you make a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th of June of this year?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you since then and while at court attested to the accuracy of that statement in front of an officer of the court?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is the statement that you produced true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May first of all for those viewing the map, the general map, at page 10 be laid on the overhead projector, and its grid reference or grid box is K and L 22 and 3 that we need to be focusing on, please. And I will read, until it comes to a material passage that has to be given live, a summary which will be a shortened form of the summary that the Chamber already has. The statement of this witness, a Kosovo Albanian born in the village of Celine, which we can see to the centre and right of the map, thank you very much, shows that he is a co-owner of a factory and a married man with three children who was awakened on the 25th of March of 1999, by an explosion sometime between 5.00 and 6.00 in the morning, following which he went to discover a Praga armoured vehicle in his yard -- not in his yard, saw from his yard a Praga armoured vehicle on the Prizren road, firing continuously into the village, with about 20 soldiers nearby. That Praga continued shelling Celine throughout the day, and women and children went to the yard of Reshit Rexhepi's house in the centre of the village, the witness observing two tanks situated on an overlooking hill. The witness, with his nephew Agim Jemini, who has already been a witness at this hearing, went to the house of Sadri Jemini, an uncle. That house was only partly completed, and the witness used a ladder to climb into a roof space, pulling the ladder up after them, the better to secure their safety. We've seen and now if I could turn to Exhibit 216, please - our copy will do for the overhead projector - we've seen already that from that top storey of a partially completed building, the witness and his nephew were able, when looking through the window opening, to have a view Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the neighbouring house within the compound and of other houses. They could hear -- or this witness could hear shelling from the Praga and the tanks. And between or sometime at about 10.00, he saw a number of shells hitting several of the houses. He also had a view from the roof by lifting a roof tile. He could see a little of what was happening outside, and he saw hundreds of MUP and VJ enter Celine from the direction of the village school on the main Prizren-Gjakove-Krusha e Madhe road. He saw the school set on fire and observed houses burning and heard the sound of continuous gunfire, seeing beneath his positions MUP and VJ personnel who spoke in Serbian. I turn from the summary to live evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, do you understand and indeed are you able, when necessary, to speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of hearing what you heard, did you hear any reference to or use of a code? If so, what code?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I heard that the code was the number 444.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear from the window opening a particular conversation that you remembered? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this a conversation between two people on the ground or in a building nearby or whatever or was it between a person and somebody being heard on a radio?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: This conversation, we were in the attic. We were able to overhear this conversation on the radio. And the number 444 was used, and the question was what was the situation like in Celine, and the answer was "The situation is all right." And the question was, "Was the massacre not a bigger one than Racak?" And the answer was, "Not only was it bigger, but the massacre was twice as big as Racak."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will come to that once more, but before I do and by reference to the photograph on the overhead projector to your left, can you explain to the Judges where the conversation was or was apparently coming from?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. In that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you point to the photograph on the projector for our assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: In this, you can't see the position where we were ourselves because we were inside the house. We were sheltering on the platform of the roof rafters, and the voices that we heard were in the lane by this house about ten metres away. And the Serbian police were positioned in this house all the time. So the conversation was heard from this house, which is near the road, and we overheard this, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The particular exchange concerning Racak, you've given us it in your own language, but just for the purposes of this trial, can you tell us, please, what you actually heard said in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. [In Serbian]: "Was it bigger than the massacre in Racak?" And the answer [In Serbian]: "It was twice as big as Racak."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the only apparently significant conversation or exchange you heard from your vantage point or did you hear other things said?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There were several conversations of this kind, and I heard others which I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to those, if I can possibly jog your memory, in a second or so, but did you stay in this position in the house?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'll come back to another -- perhaps something you overheard in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Going back to the summary, Your Honours, at the moment on page 6, although we'll go back to the last sentence on page 5, the witness's statement goes on to reveal how the MUP moved into the half completed house some 15 metres away, apparently using it as a command post. And the following morning, at about 8.00, his father, together with the parents of Agim, the earlier witness, and the witness's cousin Muharrem and his wife Zade, entered the compound. The parents of Agim or one of them, Sadri, went to the second floor and spoke with the witness and Agim through the entrance to the attic. At that stage, he was told by this witness to leave the village. Now, I turn again to live evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, in giving instructions of the kind you did to your relations through the opening in the attic roof or floor, were you concerned as to what would happen to them if they stayed in the village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you heard things that gave you reason to give them this advice?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. When Agim's father came up to us in the attic, we told him to go down because the offensive was not over, and we told him about some -- he said that the offensive was over and that people had been killed in the village, but we told him that the offensive was not over and that we had heard that it was still continuing along the Bellacerkva-Krusha e Madhe road and they had abandoned the main road and were using village roads. And we had come to the conclusion that the offensive was not yet over, and they would still be present on that section of the road. So we told them to gather in the village with other members of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any particular concerns for what might happen to people moving around in small groups? If so, why?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. We had heard something said on the radio as they talked among themselves, that anybody seen moving about in a small group of up to 10 persons would be liquidated without warning. So we understood from this that if groups were smaller, they might survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I return to the summary. I can conclude from the summary, although it touches the death of the father of this witness and I might ask him for a word or so about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following the advice you gave, were you brought food by your nephew Agim's mother, advising her --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness explains that they were brought food by Agim's mother, they advising her to leave. Shortly thereafter, a group of 20 to 30 policemen approached from the direction of Bela Crkva, burning houses as they moved, entering the yard of the witness's home and burning a house there. The group of people present, including the relations and in particular including this witness's father and the parents of Agim, with others, were brought out of a basement, robbed, asked if they had more money. Agim's father and the parents of -- Agim's father and Muharrem responded that they had money in their homes, to which they were taken to collect that money. The witness heard Agim's mother asking the policemen, "We did nothing. We are innocent. Why are you mistreating us?" The witness heard the -- a policeman tell the group to go to the side of the house, this being a group that included, of course, his own father. The group did as instructed, and the witness saw the police take up firing positions. He was unable to look. He heard a single shot followed by a burst of automatic fire. He was told thereafter by Agim what had happened. And having the courage to look, he saw a pile of bodies on the ground. The police continuing callously looting and burning houses, although they did not attempt to burn the houses, including the one in which he was hiding that was under construction. He remained in that roof space with Agim all the afternoon and evening. They saw the MUP taking away looted property on a tractor and a truck, and they heard other destruction and saw some evidence of it. At about midnight, they descended from the roof space and crawled away about the one kilometre from Celine towards Zrze. Passing the bridge at Belaja River near Bela Crkva - of which, of course, the Tribunal has heard evidence - when there, they noticed the bodies of old men, children, and younger men in the river, on the river bank and beneath the bridge, the witness estimating a group of some 30 bodies clustered together. They eventually arrived at Zrze, some five kilometres away, taking about three and a half hours to get there, Zrze appearing to be intact. With Agim, he remained at a house in that village for about two days, until on the 28th of March a fellow Celine villager, Behajdin Fetahu arrived in Zrze, telling them that the entire Celine population had been captured by Serbs in the Pisjak woods, being robbed of their valuables and identification documents. And so it was on the following day, the 29th of March that the witness, with others, went to those woods where they sheltered for the following four weeks. During the day, they remained in the woods, going to Celine for food at night, burying the bodies they found them -- found there. And he remembers burying three families in one grave, a total of 22 persons. On the last day of April, the witness and Agim joined a column of refugees and entered Albania. Later, on the 18th of June, accompanied by family and friends, he returned to Celine, where they set about the process of reburying the victims who had been buried where they'd been found. Eventually, he located the bodies of his father and Agim's parents, and they were subsequently exhumed and identified. The witness's evidence in the statement is that 82 persons were killed in Celine, of whom 75 were Celine residents and seven had gone there as guests. May the witness's 92 bis statement and associated documentation be Exhibit, and I think it's 276.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours. That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 276.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you say that you could not leave Celine on the 25th of March, 1999, because you did not have freedom of movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who restricted your freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: The Serbian police and the army restricted our freedom of movement. It was impossible to travel on the paved road from Celine to Prizren and other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In which way was this freedom of movement restricted?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: If you're talking about the time after 25th of March, it's very simple: Our movement was restricted in the sense that we couldn't even leave our house let alone go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the same page of your statement where you speak about this restriction, you say that in Celine there were many internally displaced persons from neighbouring villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how is it possible that these displaced persons came to Celine if there was no freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: These people had not been displaced after 25th of March, they had been displaced for months on end, in previous times when it had been easier to move. In our house alone, we had 24 displaced people from other villages, but they had been there for six months before the final offensive of 25th of March started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Further on, you say that between 5.00 and 6.00 in the morning the shelling of the village started, as you put it, by the Serb forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that you went into the yard and saw soldiers, vehicles. You say that soldiers were lying down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away from you were these soldiers and that vehicle that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: They were about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you see from that distance who they were shooting at, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: The -- we didn't see the soldiers that were positioned there, but we saw the armoured vehicles and the Praga firing in the direction of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But my question was whether you saw who these soldiers were shooting at.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That morning at half past five, they were shelling the village. They were only shelling the village. So that the population were trying to shelter in the woods or in different valleys. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm drawing your attention to the fact that on page 2, paragraph 7, you refer to this shooting. And in that same paragraph, you say that on that morning not a single house had been hit. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: On that morning, they shelled in order to stop the villagers fleeing the village. Their intention was to capture them all in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your comment of possible motives. I am indicating to what you said in your statement, that that morning not a single house had been hit. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That morning, they weren't hit at that time, but later they were. And I saw several houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You say, and I am reading your statement to you because you are not answering my question directly, that is paragraph 7 on this first page of the statement. Since there is a cover page, this is, in essence, the first page. You say that you saw a Praga vehicle. You say that you saw it firing continuously into the village for the entire day, with small pauses. "I did not see it hitting any houses during the morning period." So you state that they were shelling the village, and you say that they did not hit a single house. So not a single house had been hit. Is it correct that then the army and the police were responding to KLA attacks in the area, in the area of your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's not true what you say. I said before, before when the shelling started --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, say yes or no. I have many questions for you, so there's no need to elaborate. So it's not correct. They were shooting, they did not hit a single house, and they were not responding to KLA attacks. So who or what were they shooting at then? Do you know? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I can't answer your provocative questions with only yes or no. It requires an explanation. And if Your Honour will allow, I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning, at 5.30 in the morning when they started shelling, they didn't shell the houses directly. They -- they fired around the village. But later on, I saw houses in flames. So after an hour, they started shelling houses, burning houses, and the police and army infantry entered the village. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here that the soldiers were lying on the ground by the railroad, that they had taken positions because they had been attacked, and now you say that the army and police entered the village, and here you say, "I did not see any members of the MUP." So what is correct, Mr. Jemini?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think the witness has got a copy of the statement. The accused hasn't identified the passages to him. There is a habit or a pattern of putting multiple questions with the effect of confusion. The witness should have a copy of the statement, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Does he have a copy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, he apparently has one but he should have the passage brought to his attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Mr. Jemini, would you look at the seventh paragraph. It says, you will see, that between -- "At about 5.00 to 6.00, Serb forces began shelling the village," and you could see a Praga armoured vehicle parked on the main road to Prizren and soldiers deployed around it. You say the Praga was aimed towards the village and you saw it firing continuously into the village for the entire day, with small pauses. You did not see it hitting any houses, you say, during the morning period. That was the point that the accused was drawing to your attention. You now say that they started -- it started shelling the houses after an hour. You're next invited to comment on the next passage: "I saw approximately 20 soldiers near the Praga. They were just there lying on the ground near the railway track. I did not see any MUP." Now, Mr. Milosevic, what's your question about this passage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't clear. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said, the witness said, that the village had been shelled from the morning onwards and then that they did not hit a single house. Now when speaking here, he said that they were not shooting at the village but they were shooting at the surrounding area around the village, and that coincides with my question whether they were actually engaged in a conflict with the KLA that was outside the village, in the surrounding area. And then he responded to me that there was no KLA there. And then I asked him, because he said the army and the police, I asked him why he mentioned the police now when he says here, "I did not see any MUP in the -- at this stage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow the question. He said the village was attacked by the VJ and the MUP, but at this stage he's not talking about the attack, he's talking about shelling in the presence of soldiers. Now, unless you've got a question about this, let us move on. Your time will be limited, as you know, and much of it is taken up with these repetitive questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You said that the village was shelled, and now you say it was not the village that was shelled but they were shooting around the village. Now, make up your mind; was the village shelled or were they shooting around the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that question. We can see the discrepancy in his statement, and it will be a matter for us to decide what weight to give it. There's no point going on asking the same question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May. I wanted to know what the truth was finally in the witness's opinion, whether they were shooting at the village or around the village, but I never heard an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If he's given an answer, then it must be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, were you in your village, Celine, during the summer?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away is your village from Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your village can be considered the closely surrounding area of Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the period between the 17th until the 22nd of July, in the area of Orahovac, 39 Serbs and Albanians were taken away by KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at least that criminal reports were filed in this regard at the court in Prizren? And there's no point in quoting numbers of these criminal reports or anything. Have you heard about this at all, that this was reported?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I heard, but these reports were framed. We never trusted these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who is Gjelaj Hajdatoni?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I've only heard his name, and I know that he was a KLA commander, but I don't know any more about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was the leader of this gang for the area of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't know of there being any gang in the area of Rahovec, any gang of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they called it the KLA. Do you know at least that, that there was a KLA group in the area of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That was the Kosovo Liberation Army and was present not only in the Rahovec area but all over Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That much is true. And since I'm asking you about your immediate environs, do you know that the KLA intended to take over Orahovac and expel the entire non-Albanian population precisely at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that during the attack on Orahovac, they passed through your village and some KLA from your own village were involved?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There were members of the KLA from our village, but part of our village was free at that time. It means when you talk about that period, the Serbian police and the army killed more than 200 Albanians in Rahovec, and the population were forced to leave Rahovec and take refuge in safer villages, and one of these villages was Celine, where a large number of the inhabitants of Rahovec took refuge. And I have never heard of the Serbian population being expelled from Rahovec at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the KLA attack and takeover of Orahovac? Just say yes or no; "I do," or, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I have heard of confrontations, not of attacks undertaken by the KLA in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Orahovac was a strategic focus for the KLA in order to control routes towards Suva Reka, Malisevo and Prizren?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know who Skender Hoxha is?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There are a lot of people called Skender Hoxha, so I don't know this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the one who became the chief of the KLA after this failed attack on Orahovac and the death of this Hotoni. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that there had been members of the KLA from your village. Let us put that aside. But do you know that attacks of the KLA started from the direction of Djakovica and that passing through your village they forcibly mobilised a certain part of your village's inhabitants? Do you know anything about this forcible mobilisation of your locals?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There was no forced mobilisation at all. The members of the KLA were our sons, our brothers, and so we recognised and welcomed the KLA as our army. They were volunteers. Nobody was enlisted by force. There were so many volunteers that the KLA could not take them all in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is a very important statement. So you say nobody was mobilised into the KLA upon orders. Everybody was a volunteer. Tell me, since you say that you had left the village, how did you leave the village if the freedom of movement was already restricted by that time, as you put it in your statement? And how far away was this woods or the creek where the population of the village hid?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: You are talking about the period after 25th of March, 1999? Because so far you've been talking about an earlier period in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the period of 1998 first, then I moved on to the period of the NATO attack where hundreds of villagers moved away towards the woods and the creek. When the freedom of movement was restricted, as you said, how was it possible for them to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could give an answer, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not so difficult to move among the woods but it was impossible to move on the roads such as on the paved road to other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that 80 per cent of the people left their homes. Did you see with your own eyes that number of people leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: When I say 80 per cent, this is, of course, an estimate because I didn't count them. And I saw them myself. I saw all these villagers gathered, and on the 25th of March, we sent -- we sent my family too to the stream which we might call a place of refuge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are now at the -- on the attic of this house of your uncle, Sadri Jemini, and you climb up there sometime between 7.00 and 7.30; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were observing the people leaving their homes from that attic?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We could see them from the attic, but I'm talking about the period between 5.30 and 7.30. In those two hours, 80 per cent of the population of the village left the village and took shelter in safer places, either in the woods or in some stream. I saw this myself and sent my family myself to these safer places, and then I myself took shelter in the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't you go together with your family?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We didn't go because younger people were in danger if they stayed with the mass of the population. We had heard from earlier offensives that they used to divide the population, they used to separate the men from the women and children. So we knew that we would fare badly if we stayed with the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that all the men remained hidden somewhere in the village or was it just you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Some of the men were hiding, and some remained with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were you safe up there in the attic?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We thought we were safe, but it wasn't a hundred per cent safe. We thought that this attic was safer than other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how high was this attic? How roomy was it?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It was about a hundred square metres, because the house has two floors plus the attic, and the area of one floor of the house is a hundred square metres, and so the attic is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come that only the two of you hid in such a large attic?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: This happened because Agim and I - that's my cousin - we had sent our families away because we thought it was safer. But we didn't want to stay there to confront the Serbian police because it would be dangerous for us. And there were only the two of us up there in the attic because it was Agim's house. It was our house, and they wouldn't know that we were hiding up there in the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, did you have any weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, in paragraph 2, you said you saw three tanks and one Praga hitting three houses around 10.00 on the 25th of March. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you said that you are not sure who was firing. You only saw the shots being fired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We were sure that it was the Serbian police and army that was firing, but we didn't identify which tank it was that was firing on these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You stated further on that you saw a large number of policemen entering the village, and you observed all of this by raising one of the roof tiles a little, and also through a window in the attic which was upright, vertical.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you were peering through when that was safe, that you were taking quick looks when it was safe.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's true that we were in the same position all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come when we should be adjourning. It's the usual time. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, we're going to adjourn now, as you've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heard. Could you remember not to speak to anybody during the adjournment, and that includes the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in the particular circumstances of this case, the case of this witness, you can have up to another half hour with the witness, making an hour in all. Could you bear in mind the interpreters, please. I've had a message that things should be slowed down a bit for them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to finish this even sooner, because in the meantime, assuming that my time will be restricted, I eliminated some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, you said that you didn't see anyone killed on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the same paragraph, you say you overheard conversations between MUP members over the radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then on that day when you say no one was killed, you say that they claimed that it was twice as big as Racak. Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: This does make sense. But your questions are provocative. I said this: From the position where we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The questions aren't provocative. They're perfectly proper ones. Now, go on and finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the position where we were, we were unable to see who had been killed but we heard over the radio that the massacre had been twice the size of Racak. And the next day, we were told many killed people, and when we returned to the village, we identified them all, 82 people killed in the village of Celine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, to add completeness, you put that he said no one was killed that day. What his statement says is: "I did not see anyone being killed on this day. I could only hear shooting and explosions." They're rather different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely the part I quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see that anyone was killed on that day. So this lack of logic between reality and the conversation is clear. Are you clear about the use of the word "massacre"? Do you know that the word "massacre" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The premise that you put the question on is wrong. What the witness said is that he didn't see anyone killed on that day. That is different to there being nobody killed. The voice said that there was a massacre. There is no lack of logic in that. You may challenge it, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now talking, Mr. May, since I asked a question about the actual aspect of things, I'm now talking about value judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the word "massacre" was launched by William Walker?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We saw with our own eyes that massacres had taken place in Kosovo and in our village in particular. I don't know what other word we can use when a 1-year-old child is killed at its mother's breast or the most elderly people, and the bodies are burned. Some of them are totally charred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, I would appreciate it if you would only answer my questions. Do you know that the word "massacre" to us was synonymous with mass crimes, and that word was used by Walker?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It was indeed used by William Walker because that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not questioning the fact that Walker and you qualified certain things as a massacre, but do you suppose that "massacre," which for us meant mass crime, is a word that is used in their internal communications by police commanders?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means our police commanders are using your and Walker's language in their internal communications. Is that what you're asserting?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: They used their own language. They were talking in Serbian, and they put the question that I mentioned in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So somebody asks him, "Is the mass crime that you just committed bigger than the one in Racak?" You are claiming that that's what he asked him. Can you imagine such a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interrupt? The accused is trying to twist language. The witness is simply giving an account of the word he used, not of its definition or interpretation. The accused should really do better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question. That's right as a comment, Mr. Milosevic; you were just trying to twist what the witness was saying. Now, let's have the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm only pointing out that it is completely impossible that a police commander of ours had used the word "massacre," and I'm putting it to the witness that it is his invention. That's what I'm trying to clear up, and it must be clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how far away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it to the witness in terms. It's your assertion that this wasn't said. Put it to the witness in terms. I will do it. What is suggested, Mr. Jemini, is that you have invented this conversation. Now, is there any truth in that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true that I made it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how far away were you from the house from which you heard this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I was only 15 metres away. But the lane that goes through the villages of Bellacerkva, Krusha e Madhe, Celine is only ten metres away from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, since you are saying that shelling was going on at that time, shooting, racket, how come that with all this -- or, rather, through all this racket and shooting, yelling, and so on and so forth you can still overhear a conversation?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Very easily. They talked about a lot of other things that we didn't hear, but what we heard was during a pause in the shelling and shooting, and at that time we could hear the conversation clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to hear even what the person on the other side of the line, the radio line, was saying. You heard not only the person who was 15 metres away from you but also his interlocutor on the other side. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That's true. It was a radio link that you could hear very clearly, and you could hear the other side very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You are saying that they were located on the second floor of that house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: They were on the second floor, but they also moved. And they were on the first floor, and they came into our house too, as far as the second floor. And you could also hear conversations on the street nearby when they passed, from the attic of the house, which was only ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You stated you had to lie down. You were afraid to move around the attic and that once or twice you raised the roof tile and peered through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: The truth is that we were 42 hours in that attic, and during those 42 hours, we were sometimes lying down, we were sometimes sitting up, and we were sometimes standing, and we sometimes looked out to see what was happening round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. But practically, in view of your position, you were not able to see who or why or at whom they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's not true what you say. We saw the members of our families when they fired on them and when they killed -- and -- but from the position where we were, the other families were further away, and we couldn't see who was killed and who was not. And it was later, when we came to bury them, that we managed to identify the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that. From that attic during the night, you heard the noise made by a tractor, and you heard people living the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could they move around when movement was impossible? And moreover, you say that they were moving on tractors. I suppose the police must have heard that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we heard the tractors, it was 1.00 in the morning, and it was a position above the village. So they were moving from the village to the woods. And the police weren't up there because they were -- had no doubt no security for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. But on the 26th, in the morning - we're not talking about the woods now - you said your father came up to the attic, into your house, that is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: On the next day, on the 26th at 8.00 in the morning, my uncle, not my father, came to the house, and not to the attic but to the floor below, and spoke to us through the aperture that we used to enter the loft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Uncle or father, that's not the point here. How was he able to reach you if the police had a command post in the house next to you and movement was forbidden?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I said this; after 1.00 in the morning, all the shelling stopped until 9.00 the next morning. And he didn't know what was happening in our house, and he was concerned about our fate, and that was why he had come up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not asking why he came. I asked how could he possibly come under the circumstances that you described, that there was no freedom of movement and that the police were in the house next door, et cetera. That means that there was freedom of movement; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: You can call it freedom of movement. It wasn't freedom of movement at all. It was merely luck that he wasn't fired on. And at that time, the police were not in position. And after 9.00, they came back to the house where they had been before. But during that time, at the position where they had been on the Prizren-Gjakove road and above the school, there were armoured vehicles stationed, but down below in the village they didn't notice this and they thought the offensive was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not when I asked you. You are talking about this freedom of movement and about the movement, you say that Agim's mother came and brought you food. So her movement through the village was unhindered as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's true that people were moving, but those people who were in movement did suffer consequences, like the members of my family. Because people who went out fared worse, like my own parents. I don't know what you mean by "freedom of movement."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just asked you how your uncle came, how Agim's mother came to bring food, et cetera, because you said that nobody could move about. It seems that you were the only one who was hiding. That's the way it's been put. Now let me skip a few questions. You heard fire from automatic weapons, and you say that some people were taken out by the house.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, there were shots, and our relatives, my parents, were taken out of the house. My father, my uncle, my uncle's wife, and my cousin and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see somebody kill them? Did you see somebody shoot at them?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We saw the entire incident. They had been sheltering in a basement when the police came. The police came and got them out of the basement, and the first question was, "Do you have money? Do you have any money?" And they replied, said that they did. And indeed, my father had 10.000 Swiss francs. And I don't know how much my uncle had and my cousin, but all the money they had in their pockets was taken. And then they asked, "Do you have any more money hidden at home?" My uncle said that he did, and they went into his house. And my cousin, Muharrem, and his wife, they took his money as well, thinking that by giving them money they might save their own lives. And then they gathered them altogether, all five of them, and at that moment, Agim's mother turned round and said, "What are you doing? We've done nothing. What are you doing to us?" And then they took them behind the house, lined them up. I saw this with my own eyes. They took up position to shoot, and at that moment I didn't have the strength to watch because I knew what was happening. And I fell down, lying, and Agim remained standing and watched them being shot. I heard the volley of gunfire, and Agim confirmed to me that they had been killed. After a short time, I stood up, too, and I saw their bodies lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood your statement to mean that you had seen their bodies but that you did not see when they had been killed. Now you've explained it somewhat differently. So where were you in the attic? Could you see from that place where you were the place where they were allegedly executed?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see the execution.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: The moment of execution, I didn't see that because I didn't have the strength to see what was happening to my parents. It's not easy to see your parents being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, on page 6 you mention that on the 30th of March, you talked to some men in the Pisjak forest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these men members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of April, you went to Albania; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you there with the members of your family?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Then we met our relatives in Albania. Except, of course, for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that Muharrem and Zade Jemini's body were charred; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that these bodies were never officially identified; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: These bodies, when we got back from Albania, we asked for them. We asked the members of the Tribunal to investigate them because some had been buried in Rahovec and others were at home and others were charred. And then we suspected that the identity of these carbonised bodies and the Tribunal experts proved that these people had been killed and burned and only some bones of them were left. And we assumed that nobody else was missing among the ranks of our relatives. There's no other way of identifying them because we are only left with some bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 6 you say that you buried a total of 22 persons. How did you find out -- on the basis of what did you conclude that 82 had been killed if you had only buried 22?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's not true. It's nowhere in my statement that we buried only 22. There were 22 buried in one mass grave alone, and there are others buried in ones, twos, threes, and fives. They were killed in the houses, they were killed in cellars, they were killed in yards, and some were buried where they died, because even as we were burying them, we were not safe. We had no safety at this time. This, of course, we did during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see the circumstances under which these persons were killed and who killed them?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: They were killed by the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you whether you saw this or whether this is what you've been claiming on the basis of what you think.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: At that moment, there were no other armed forces in our village. We saw our parents being killed by Serbian police and army forces, and so the other people who were killed were also killed by the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that none of these people were killed in the fighting between the army and police and the KLA? Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We believe that nobody was killed in the confrontation between the KLA and the Serbian police and army but directly by the Serbian forces, because the Kosovo Liberation Army were very few at that moment. And considering the weaponry that was round the village and the size of the Serbian forces, they didn't want to put the population in danger, and so they withdrew for the population's sake. And there was not a single shot fired between the KLA and the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that none of the persons killed that you refer to was a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There was only one who was a soldier of the KLA, and he was killed in a wood near the village while he was giving up his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is my conclusion on the basis of everything that you've been saying correct, that you personally had not seen a single killing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I've said it several times, and I saw five people, including my parents, killed. I don't know how you can say nobody in the light of these five people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have only a few questions for Mr. Jemini.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jemini, in connection with something that you described in your statement on page 1, you said that in Celine, there were many internally displaced persons. When saying "internally displaced persons," do you mean persons who fled from the areas where there were conflicts between the police and the KLA, that people then sought shelter at safer places, and then for a period of six months stayed in your village as well?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No, that's not right. The Serbian police used to enter villages where people had been expelled and were taking shelter and had expelled these displaced people in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were they in danger of anyone there in Celine while they were staying with you?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Not only they were in danger but we were in danger too, but we were in less danger than in the villages from which they had been expelled because Serbian forces had still not entered our village at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain how you were in danger and how they were in danger and how many persons were there from other villages?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of people from other villages, but about 2.000 from other villages was -- were in Celine, and Celine has 2.500 inhabitants. So I suppose there must have been about 4.500 to 5.000 people gathered in Celine at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on page 1, you say that on the 24th of March, 1999, you heard the sound of aircraft above you and that you saw a fire then in the direction of Prizren. Was that during the night, this bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: That was about 8.00 in the evening on 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was some more bombing in the area where Celine is?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: There was bombing near Celine in places where there were concentrations of Serbian forces, with heavy vehicles belonging to the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Nogavac from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Only one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this village was bombed during the first days of April? Do you know what happened? Do you know who actually did the bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I know that on the night before Nagafc was bombed we had been there. But later, we were not in Nagafc but in Celine, whereas in Nagafc at about 2.00 in the morning, a very loud explosion was heard, and even from where we were, we could hear something and we could hear that it was very close. One person who was with us in the group in Celine had been in Nagafc that night and came to Celine and confirmed that Nagafc had been shelled during the night. But he said that they were -- it was bombed by planes that flew very low. And later it was demonstrated that these were planes belonging to the Serbian army, because there was a very large number of people taking refuge in that village, perhaps more than 8.000 people. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to all of that, did you hear that there were ten craters that were ten by seven? The craters from the bombs, that is. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: I have heard, but I wasn't really concerned about their dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. You spent 42 hours in the attic; is that right? That's the way you put it. When you decided to leave the attic, did you take a look? Did you see whether there was anybody nearby and was it only then that you decided to leave the place where you had been?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Before we left -- when we left, it was 1.00 in the morning when all the shelling had stopped. And seeing that all the houses in our yard and more than 80 per cent of the village had been burned - and I saw this with my own eyes - I heard that our village, our house would be burnt too, and so this was why we left the attic. So that as we left, we were quite unable to see much because it was dark, and also, there was rain that night. We set off in the direction of Zrze.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, could you just explain this, because your nearest and dearest lost their lives before your very own eyes. Did you walk up perhaps to see whether they were showing any signs of life or did you not walk up to them? Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: The -- we had watched the bodies now and then during the entire day, and they had never moved. And at the moment when we left, the bodies were directly opposite a Serbian police position, and we could not go up to them, so we went around them in quite a different direction and left the village that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only an incomplete part of your account about burying bodies has been summarised by the accused. Is the position, as set out in your statement as follows, page 6: That the 22 people you buried in a single grave included three families comprising respectively seven, six, and five individuals for each family, together with some other bodies of other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.
