utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two bodies whose remains were charred were actually found by you in your own yard or compound, and for the reasons that you've given, they were never fully identified but you calculated, because you've never seen them since and there weren't any other bodies, that they were Muharrem and Zade Jemini; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We supposed that there were no others there, and so -- and others were accounted for, so we came to the conclusion that these people were Muharrem and Zade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In addition to those, and working with other people including the relation from whom we have heard, were the total of 82 people buried that were buried, either all or very nearly all of them, in a graveyard dedicated specifically to that purpose in your village, with appropriate markers over each individual grave? Is that correct now?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It's correct. We identified the people who were buried because there were people of the village who buried them, and we also marked each grave and put a name in a bottle on each grave and put the bottles on the grave so that when we came back from Albania they were all marked and it was easier to complete the task of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There has been some veiled question but no positive suggestion about some force other than the Serb forces killing these people. Has there been any suggestion in the area where you live that forces other than the Serbian forces killed any of these 82 people from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: No. There were no other forces besides the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There have been some questions asked of you about your staying separated from your family before they were killed. From your knowledge of what happened at that time, would it have added to the safety of your family for you, the younger men, to have stayed with them when they were at risk in the way you identify?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: It would have been much more dangerous, because in earlier offensives, people above 20 and middle-aged people were separated from their families and executed. So to avoid a worse fate, we thought that the best thing we could do would be to hide in that loft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, and it hasn't been challenged by the accused, you spoke of hearing instructions given that people moving around in small groups should be killed. We haven't had a precise count of the number of people including your father and other relations who were killed, but was it more or less than ten? If you can give us the precise number, please do so.

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: We heard that anybody moving in small groups of up to ten people should be liquidated without warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the group including your parents or your father, as you described it sometimes, was that more or less than ten?

utterances.speaker: ISUF JEMINI
utterances.text: Later, when we found the people who had been killed in groups, groups of two, five, ten, and then up to 22, but then there were also individuals who were killed. In total, there were 82 people killed in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, that concludes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. May, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Nice said that I did not challenge some conversation about groups. I challenged his ability to hear any conversation at all so I don't think that I should challenge every word that was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jemini, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the international Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness has been identified for some time as K34, a pseudonym. In fact, as we were informed by his lawyer who has been representing him for reasons that will become apparent, he's happy to give evidence in open session and with his name known. Indeed, one of the characteristics of this case applies in his case as well; his name has, in any event, been publicised as a potential witness associated with the pseudonym in the territory. So I call Radomir Markovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness stand to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Radomir Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Markovic, were you formerly the head of state security for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the head of the state security of Serbia from the -- from November 1998 to year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your present position, as revealed in part by the circumstances in which you entered this room, is that you are still on trial in Serbia in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trial that has yet to be completed, and as is well known in Serbia, a charge that includes counts of murder laid against you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Allegations that you are contesting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I'm contesting them. I was falsely accused in Serbia, and I hope that justice will prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First may we deal with your background, and to some of these questions yes/no answers will probably be permitted and may save time. Were you born in 1946 in Lukavac in Bosnia, educated in Belgrade, graduating from the law faculty there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had your entire professional life been spent working for the MUP, which you joined in 1970, working for the first five years as an operative in the second department of the management for criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then spend eight years at the department for the prevention of drug trafficking, subsequently becoming head of department at Belgrade airport?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then became head of public security in the city of Belgrade and indeed secretary of security for that city?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You became an Assistant Minister of the Interior in two separate departments, the later one of which was -- or the first one of which was for analytical and informational works and the latter one of which was as Assistant Minister for Criminal Acts.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then that brings us to November 1998, when you became head of the state security branch, the RDB of the MUP. Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to that position by the Minister of the Interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if any, part in that appointment did the accused take?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I presume that it was the suggestion of Slobodan Milosevic, but I cannot know that with certainty. I was nominated by Vlajko Stojiljkovic. I suppose that the president was aware of that and that he approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn now to the chain of command operative at the time you were performing this job. To whom did you report as head of state security?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that a chain of command that -- or was reporting to him within a legally established chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was in keeping with the legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your instructions came from whom, from the same minister or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From the minister. We had regular staff meetings where the minister issued us assignments for the period that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to form a view one way or the other as to how the instructions you received from the minister fitted with the policies of the president, the accused?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the policy of a country is charted by the president together with his associates, and the Minister of the Interior certainly has to follow that policy. There is no doubt about that. So the state policies are created by state authorities and the president of that state, and we were only executive bodies who followed the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever yourself report directly to the accused?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In what sense did you mean "report"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Report on what you were doing, on your actions, tell him what you were engaged in; did you ever report to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic received daily reports both from the public security and the state security branches. And when he was particularly interested in something, he would invite me to his office and I would have to elaborate on that either in the form of a written report or verbally, depending on his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the detail of weekly reporting in a little while's time. You took over your position from whom, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he somebody you knew well or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know Jovica Stanisic very well. I knew him superficially as a colleague, as a professional, not socially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you seen a document dealing with the control of or subordination of Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw such a document. It was shown to me by Jovica Stanisic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And roughly when did he show you this document that you can now recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he showed it to me immediately after I took over from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the date of the document, or at any rate, the year, if you can recall, of the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I can. I believe it was 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now please see the document, which we will produce as an exhibit. On this occasion, I think it may be desirable for the whole four-sheet package to be before the Court, which includes the explanation of how this document comes to be provided to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can do the following, please, Mr. Usher: If we can look at -- first of all view the first page briefly so that those viewing can see what it is. First of all in the -- it's proper to see it in the original and then we'll go to the English. So we a document, a letter with a stamp in Cyrillic, and the second page is then -- if you turn over, please. The next document is a document in Cyrillic, and we can see at the foot of it a date, 21st of April, 1997, and again some official stamps. If we go to the third sheet, please, we come to the translation of those documents in order, the first being a letter from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dated the 27th of June, addressed to the liaison officer, Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, signed by the assistant federal minister, and following the formal courtesies, forwarding, it says in the second or third line, forwarding to this Tribunal, or the office of the Prosecutor in any event, a copy of the decision DT numbered 1/97 from the 21st of April, that was brought by the former president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic. And then we can see a translation on the fourth sheet of the document itself. And the document reads: "According to the Article 83 of the Republic of Serbia constitution, I bring the following..." I should observe it's headed "State secret." "Decision. 1. During the preparations for passing the law on carrying out the security affairs of the FR Yugoslavia, the department of the state security will perform its duties in accordance with the guidelines of the president of the republic and the Republic of Serbia government. As from this day, this decision is put into effect until the day the federal law is enforced, which shall, in accordance with the constitution of the FR Yugoslavia, regulate the security affairs in the framework of the FR Yugoslavia jurisdiction. "2. This decision is put into effect on the day it was brought." And then signed by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, just having seen this document, I think today, can you help us one way or another whether this is the same document that you were shown by Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document thus says that the department of state security will perform its duties in accordance with guidelines of the president of the republic and the Republic of Serbia government until the federal law that it sets out is enforced. First, was the relevant federal law referred to there ever made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was just a bill that was never enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So as long as it was in effect, this decision of the accused had the effect of bringing the department of state security under his control?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in effect only during the tenure of Jovica Stanisic, because when I took over as head of the state security branch, that was no longer in effect. It no longer applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with it in two stages: Until the end of Stanisic's term of office, it was in effect.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From the day of the entry into force of this decision until the end of his term of office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say it didn't apply in your case. Is there any document recording the cancellation of this order or decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if such a document exists. I was informed of that by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, who told me that the state security branch had to address directly the Ministry of the Interior, that is, him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of this decision and through to the time of your holding this office, was there any federal State Security Service or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The federal State Security Service did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the Republic of Serbia's security service was performing the task of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You could put it that way. But it is not completely accurate. Since that had not been agreed with the Ministry of the Interior of Montenegro, it functioned only partially, to the extent that was necessary for security of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So now can we turn to the process of meetings, briefings, and reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this will take us beyond a quarter to. I don't know what additional time is required for the arrangements of the witness, given the circumstances in which he arrives here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be better to start tomorrow on that. Mr. Markovic, we're going to adjourn now. Would you remember during this adjournment until we recommence your evidence tomorrow, and indeed any other adjournments there may be, not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes speaking to members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of July, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
